text: 7:45. Today's calendar: a tasting at the bakeries, a release at the software firm, the transfer window at the club and a delayed flight. What comes first?
right: The release, at least it's on fire

text: At 6 a.m. the head of your bakery chain sends a photo of a new baguette captioned "This is a breakthrough." It looks like a regular baguette. Your reply?
Your jet pilot texts: "Departure delayed, waiting for a slot. Estimated time: eventually." Your meeting in another city is at noon. How do you get there?
right: Wait for the jet, however long

text: Your nephew calls over breakfast: "I want to work at the football club. Any job. Ideally a boss job." He has zero experience. What do you say?
left: Get him an internship at the ticket desk

text: You wake up unable to remember whether you own seven companies or eight. You think you bought something yesterday. Check?
Your media outlet's editor wants to front-page a story about problems at… your own airline. "We're an independent publication." Your move?
The coach is waiting at the door with a tablet: "We need a new striker. Urgently. Here's the video." The video is forty minutes long. Watch it?
right: "Send me three numbers, not a video"

text: The family office sent your weekly schedule. Not one free hour, but there's a "lunch with yourself — 15 minutes" slot. What do you do?
left: Fight for a full lunch hour
right: Accept it, 15 minutes is still lunch

text: The airline's director wants to repaint the planes in the holding's colours. There are four planes, and the paint job costs about as much as a fifth. Approve?
Three of your company directors are sitting in reception, each sure the meeting is theirs. According to the calendar, there's one meeting. Who goes in?
The head of your software firm texts at 7 a.m.: "The server went down, but good news: we found out we have no backup." Reply?
right: "Why am I hearing this only now?"

text: Your driver suggests skirting the traffic through the industrial zone where your new bakery warehouse is. "You can take a look while we're there." Stop in?
Your charity foundation asks you to speak at a library opening at 9:00. At 9:30 there's a club board meeting across town. What now?
The head baker reports that someone from holding management ate the whole batch of test croissants. The security footage shows you. Explanation?
right: Apologise and bake a new batch together

text: The holding's treasurer asks whose budget pays for the jet repair: the airline's, the holding's, or "your personal happiness." Decide.
Your sister calls: "You own bakeries, right? I need a cake for a hundred people for my birthday. Free — we're family." Reply?
The captain asks you to come to morning training "for motivation." Training's at six. It's ten to six now.
left: Show up in a suit and yell "Come on!"
right: Record a voice note for the locker room

text: A buyer offers good money for your media company, on one condition: fire all the journalists. "We only need the brand." Your answer?
The club director wants sign-off on a striker who costs as much as the bakeries earn in a year. The bakery director is accidentally cc'd.
left: Approve it, the club comes first

text: The lawyer brings a 140-page contract for buying a small toy factory. "At least read the risk section." It's forty pages long.
Live on air, an anchor from your own channel said your football club "plays like it's their first time." The club demands an on-air apology. What now?
right: Invite the club to reply on air

text: Your cousin wants to "invest in the holding" an amount that would buy one bicycle. In return, he wants a board seat.
right: Invite him to a board meeting as a guest

text: The auditor found your airline buys passenger coffee from your own bakeries above market price. "That's a conflict of interest." What do you do?
The bakery and airline directors are arguing over whose logo goes on the in-flight lunch box. Both want your ruling right in the chat.
The jet's flight attendant asks if the youth football team can fill the empty seats for an away game. It'll take up your evening.
Your software firm wants one app for all your businesses: buy a bun, a match ticket and a flight in one place. Sounds odd. Green light?
left: A small budget for a pilot
right: "Let's do buns on their own first"

text: The banker insists: "Sell the airline while someone still wants it." You love those four planes, late as they are. Your call?
Club fans hung a banner: "Owner, where are the signings?!" It's right next to your bakery, and the queue there is growing. Reaction?
left: Go out to the fans with buns

text: At lunch you catch yourself thinking about five companies at once while eating soup from your own bakery that you haven't actually tasted. Pause?
The CFO shows a chart: everything's growing except the football club, which declines so smoothly it almost looks pretty. What about the club?
Your mum calls mid-meeting: "I watched the weather on your channel and the presenter had no scarf. Tell them that won't do." Now what?
left: Pass it on to the editor, smiling
right: Tell Mum you're in a meeting

text: You're offered a small ski resort. The owner swears there's snow "almost always." The video he sent shows grass.
The group HR director wants a single culture across all companies. Bakers, coders and footballers would all wear the same hoodie.
right: Let each keep its own style

text: A journalist asks if it's true you bought the football club "just because you love football." It is. But it sounds unserious. Your answer?
7:30 p.m. The jet is finally ready — six hours late. The meeting you were flying to already happened on a video call. Fly anyway?
At dinner your daughter asks: "Will I run the holding when I grow up?" She's nine. The whole table freezes. Your answer?
Your club lost 0–4. The director calls: "You need to say something in the dressing room." You know nothing about tactics. What do you say?
left: "I believe in you. Get some rest"
right: Promise bonuses for the next game

text: Your spouse reminds you it's your anniversary. At the holding, the toy factory deal signs at 9 p.m. What do you do?
right: Sign and make it for dessert

text: In the group chat of all your company directors someone posts "Good night, everyone!" and for forty minutes everyone politely replies the same. You're reading.
At 10 p.m. the editor sends tomorrow's headline: "Holding owner misses own plane again." That's you. It's true.
Instead of sheep, you're counting subsidiaries to fall asleep. At number seven you realise you can't remember one of them at all. Now what?
The airline director says passengers praise the meals from your bakeries more than the flights. "Maybe sell the meals without the flights?"
Your teenage son wants a summer job at your software firm, "but nobody can know I'm your kid." How do you help?
right: Quietly ask someone to keep an eye

text: The foundation manager asks you to personally sign two hundred thank-you cards for volunteers. "It'll mean a lot from the owner." It's 9 p.m.
The coach messages at night: "If we don't buy a defender, I'm out." Third time this season. Reply now?
right: Call him now and talk him down

text: Your assistant asks whether to book the jet tomorrow, or the train straight away "in case the jet does its thing again." Decide.
The bakery director sent a long evening email about feeling undervalued compared with the football club. It includes photos of pies.
left: Invite him to lunch and listen

text: For the first time in a month you have a free evening. No calls, no flights. You can't remember what people do with free evenings.
The buyer of your software firm calls at 11 p.m. and raises the offer by ten percent — if you answer before midnight. No time to sleep on it.
The office security guard, last to leave, asks whether to switch off the lights in your office. You're still in it. It's past ten.
The director of your newly bought toy factory greets you with a box: "The first plush mascot for your club!" It looks like a sad potato. Launch it?
right: Send it back for a redesign

text: Grandma calls at 7:10 asking why cheese buns went up at her favourite bakery. It's your bakery. She knows.
Your assistant asks which of your five company mugs goes on your desk today. "The other directors are watching." Which one?
right: Set up a mug rotation schedule

text: The coders want to come to the office only on Wednesdays. Your other companies already heard and want the same rule. Your call?
left: Allow it for the coders only
right: Let each company decide for itself

text: The airline dispatcher reports the morning flight is delayed because the pilot is stuck in traffic behind your car. Yours.
left: Get out and wave him ahead

text: The family lawyer wants to start talking succession. "No rush, but better now than on the run." You're on the run.
Your trainer's been waiting at the gym since 7:00. You, at 7:00, are reading revenue reports from five companies. Pick one.
The head baker asks to bake bread shaped like the software firm's logo for its anniversary. "Three hundred loaves with a cursor on top." Approve?
The captain posted a morning video of you whiffing a penalty at a charity match. A hundred thousand views. What now?
right: Ask him to take it down

text: The treasurer wants all companies on one bank "to keep it simple." Three of your company heads object. Your call?
Your uncle turns up unannounced with an idea: "A bakery inside a plane! Fresh bread at altitude!" He's drawn it on a napkin.
The driver asks if he can hang the club pennant in the car. The club lost two days ago, and people honk at you at traffic lights. Hang it?
The new manager of the hotel you bought last week calls at 8:00: "Is someone supposed to tell me what to do?"
The pilot says the jet is ready on time. First time in a year. You're still at home in pyjamas, departure in forty minutes.
right: Push it back — for tradition's sake

text: HR wants an 8:00 directors' meeting every Monday. Half the directors are in another time zone.
right: Every Monday, join if you can

text: The foundation received thirty scholarship applications and wants you to read the finalists. Twelve of them, five-page essays each.
The head of your media company wants a morning show with you hosting once a week. "People want a real-life owner." You can't do early mornings.
right: Decline, leave it to the pros

text: The club director wants to name the stadium after your holding. Fans have already started a petition: "Keep the old name."
The software firm wants to build demand forecasting for the bakeries. The bakers say they already know: more buns on Fridays.
The owner of a rival holding invites you to lunch "just to chat." Everyone knows he wants to buy your club.
Accounts asks how to book the toy plane you bought for pocket change at a kiosk for the airline's meeting room.
The coach asks you to stop coming to games: "When you're in the stands, the lads get nervous." You bought the club to go to games.
The airline director wants to launch a route to the small town where you grew up. Profits are doubtful, but your mum will be thrilled.
You're having lunch in your own bakery and the cashier doesn't recognise you. Payment, please. You only have the holding's company card.
The lawyer warns that buying the ski resort also gets you an old lift and three stubborn goats. The goats are in the contract.
right: Rehome the goats at a farm

text: The bakery director wants a bakery right inside the stadium. The club director objects: "We have hot dogs. They're tradition."
left: Open the bakery next to them

text: A journalist from another outlet wants an interview on "what it's like to own everything." You own five companies and a cactus.
The board wants fewer companies: "You can't keep up." They suggest selling two. Which ones?
The editor wants a bigger investigations budget. "We'll find what's being hidden." The board worries they'll find something of yours.
An investor offers to buy 51% of your bakeries. Big money, but he'll be deciding the recipes.
Your assistant made you a lunch from all your companies: bakery bread, airline coffee, a sweet with the club logo. Together it's odd.
The bakers want a higher night-shift bonus. The footballers just got a bonus for a draw. The bakers noticed.
Your sister wants a column at your media outlet about "living with a tycoon sibling." You're not a tycoon.
The hotel director wants to keep a permanent "owner's suite." You visit that city once a year.
You finally arrived on time, but your luggage stayed in another city. It flew with your own airline. File a complaint?
Your son needs help with homework: "Describe your parents' business." He asks how much he can copy from your annual report.
left: Tell it like a bedtime story

text: The club director calls after a loss: "The fans want the coach fired. The coach wants the fans fired."
Your channel won an award for honest journalism. At the ceremony they thank you "for not interfering." Go on stage?
right: Go up and give a speech

text: Your spouse asks if, just for the weekend, you could leave behind the three phones — one per company.
The toy factory got a big holiday order. Three night shifts in a row. The director asks if you'll come by to cheer them on.
The pilot offers to drop you home "on the way" — a 200 km detour. The train is tomorrow morning.
After his first day as a club cashier, your nephew writes: "That was hard. Can I be director now?"
left: Tell him to last a month
right: Invite him to dinner and listen

text: The flight attendant asks what to order for tomorrow's flight. You're not sure tomorrow's flight will happen at all.
Evening: your club's match, the software firm's report and your outlet's news, all on three screens at once. You understand none of it.
left: Turn off all but the match

text: The foundation asks you to read a story to kids in a hospital on Saturday. Saturday is also the cup final with your club playing.
left: The story — watch the replay later

text: At 10:30 p.m. the treasurer sends expenses listing "empty jet flight" four times. You weren't on any of them.
left: Sort it out with the pilot tomorrow

text: Your daughter wants "a little airline like yours" for her birthday. She's turning ten.
11 p.m., from the software CEO: "We've got an idea that'll change the holding! Talk at seven tomorrow?" Your tomorrow already starts at seven.
At 9 p.m. the bakery director reports an entire night shift is off sick at one shop. There'll be a bread queue at dawn. Who bakes?
Mum watches your channel and calls: "Why are you on the news in a crumpled jacket again? Iron it tomorrow."
Morning meeting at the outlet. The editor asks if they can cover your bakery winning an award. "Won't it look like an ad?"
The coach wants a new heated pitch. In the photo, the old one has a bald patch shaped like a heart.
right: Keep the heart for a season

text: The hotel director reports every room is booked by fans of the rival team. Rival to your club. They're already singing.
Your assistant suggests arriving at the software firm's meeting on a scooter: "They'll appreciate it." You got one as a gift. Never ridden it.
The bakery director sent a poll: which new doughnut flavour — "Football," "Aviation," or "Holding." Nobody knows what they mean.
right: Ask what the flavours actually are

text: The pilot says departure is delayed because catering delivered the wrong bread — "from a competitor." Wait for your own bakery's bread?
Morning. Inbox: forty emails from directors, two from family, one from the foundation and one titled "URGENT!!!" from someone unknown. Start where?
The airline director wants to name morning flights after holding employees. The first one would carry your name.
The family office asks what share of income goes to the foundation this year. Last year was five percent; the board suggests less.
A new coder messages you directly: "Hi, are you really the owner? Can I ask about football?"
right: Gently mention the chain of command

text: The treasurer proposes one staff card with discounts across all companies. The pilots ask if it works for doughnuts.
Your uncle's back. Now he wants a "football club for retirees." He'd be the coach.
left: Give him the pitch an hour a week

text: The morning anchor wants your comment on flight delays. Your channel, your airline, your delays.
Your trainer suggests working out at your club's stadium. The groundskeepers and the youth squad will be watching.
Group HR wants a "gratitude morning": every director publicly thanks a director from another company. The directors are tense.
The driver suggests picking up the head baker, who's late for his shift. You're late for negotiations.
The buyer wants to see your bakeries "as a regular customer." He walks into the one where the till broke today.
left: Own it and show him another

text: The board wants a group managing director so you're not doing everything. The candidate is your long-time rival.
The club director wants you to personally call a player they want to sign. "The owner's attention matters to him." He's nineteen.
left: Call and chat like a human

text: The head baker refuses to make "startup bread" — gluten-free with added caffeine. "That's not bread, it's a drink."
right: Ask him to at least try

text: The lawyer wants each company in its own legal entity "so if one falls, the others don't notice." Sad but sensible.
The airline wants to sell your factory's toys on board. The factory director is thrilled; the cabin crew horrified.
The CFO shows you spent more on the jet this quarter than the foundation spent on scholarships. It'll show in the annual report.
Your cousin opened a café and wants your bakeries to supply her bread. With payment due "sometime later."
A rival holding is poaching your head baker with double pay. He came to tell you honestly.
At lunch you realise you've been to five cities this week but can't remember eating in any of them. Fifth sandwich this week.
left: Sit down in a café properly
right: Sandwich on the run, as always

text: The software firm wants to go public in two years. The CEO asks for your approval — and personal advice on wearing a tie.
Fans demand the old striped kit back. The new one, they say, looks like pyjamas. New kits are already bought.
The foundation wants a free summer coding school at your software firm. The coders fear they'll have to teach.
The toy factory wants to release a "Holding Owner" doll. It comes with three phones and a suitcase.
A bank offers a growth loan for all your companies — secured against the football club. The fans won't like it.
Your assistant found two interviews booked at the same time today: one for your channel, one for a rival's.
The editor asks you for a column on humility. You're writing it on the jet. It shows.
Evening: a young player scored his first goal and dedicated it to "the person who bought us a bus." That's you.
Your spouse suggests a holiday free of all your businesses: no hotel, no plane, no bakeries. "Just a tent."
The head baker brings you a loaf of new bread in the evening: "You're the first to taste it." Bank call in five minutes.
You close the laptop and instantly remember you never replied to the airline director. He's been waiting since lunch.
The pilot calls: "The jet's in repair again. Good news — the mechanics say they've never seen anything like it."
Your son became a school celebrity because your club won. Now his whole class wants tickets.
10 p.m.: the editor asks if tomorrow's edition should report your rival buying a newspaper. "We are a news outlet."
Charity auction night. Your lot: "dinner with the holding's owner." No one is raising a paddle.
Leaving for the night, your assistant leaves a note: "Please don't buy anything tonight." You're browsing a listing for an ice rink.
The hotel director invites you to an evening with guests in the restaurant. Guests want selfies with the owner. You want to go home.
The coach sends tomorrow's tactics and asks your opinion. Arrows and circles. You can see a smiley face.
The treasurer says there's one holiday gift budget for all. Three hundred bakers, forty coders. How to split it?
Falling asleep, you think: "What if we bought a circus too?" Fifth idea this week.
left: Write it down and forget it

text: Late evening: a flight's delayed and passengers in the lounge are singing your club's anthem. Good sign or bad?
Your niece sends her college essay: "My relative owns a holding, which taught me…" She wants feedback. The relative is you.
left: Help her write you out of it

text: A board member sends a "quick question" at 9:40 p.m. It's three pages on strategy to 2040.
The toy factory sends a video: the night shift finished its first thousand toy cars and is dancing. They invite you to join on video.
The ski resort manager calls at 6:30: "It snowed! But the lift froze." Tourists arrive at nine.
The head of a laundry chain you bought "by accident" with a building asks for her first meeting. You forgot you owned laundries.
Your assistant proposes a new rule: no director calls before 9:00. The airline director is calling. It's 8:12.
At 6 a.m. the bakers set you a test: taste which bread is yours and which is from a supermarket. Everyone's watching.
The club director proposes a stadium open day where anyone can talk to the owner. There's already a queue.
right: Come out for half an hour

text: You wake up in a hotel and can't tell if it's yours or someone else's. The slippers have no logo.
right: Look for a logo on the towels

text: The family lawyer brings a draft succession plan. The "successor" field is blank, but someone pencilled in "the cat."
The pilots suggest a morning stretch session for passengers on flights. The director is unsure. You?
Dad advises: "Sell everything but the bakeries. People always need bread." He's said it every Monday for ten years.
The software CEO wants you to address staff about "the vision." Your vision is that the release ships on Friday.
Office security won't let you in — you forgot your pass. The guard is new and trying hard.
Your channel wants morning weather reports from the ski resort. "Synergy!" It's your resort. No snow yet.
The treasurer reports the laundries are more profitable than the football club. Five times more. Tell the club director?
The flight attendant asks what music to play at take-off. Three company directors flying with you want different things.
Your cousin texts: "Get me a job at the airline. I love flying." His experience: one flight as a passenger, twelve years ago.
left: Point him to cabin crew training

text: The foundation wants approval to fund a dog shelter. The club director asks for "a little too" for a new bus.
You bought a farm so your bakeries could use your own flour. The farm director says the wheat's great, but the mill has been broken since 1987.
The banker presents "Holding 2.0": sell everything but tech. The bakery slide is crossed out in red.
Your small cinema's director wants to show club matches on the big screen. The club director fears no one will come to the stadium.
The bakeries are launching delivery. The director wants scooter couriers in the club's colours. The club has lost three in a row.
Queuing at your own bakery, you hear customers gossiping: "They say the owner's never here."
right: Stay quiet and buy a bun

text: HR proposes a swap: the bakery director runs the airline for a month, and vice versa. "Fresh eyes."
The board wants a one-page report per company. The club's begins: "It's been a tough season."
You're offered a bookshop chain. The seller cries while calling it his life's work. The price is double what it's worth.
The captain asks: the team wants to play a charity match against the bakers for the foundation. The bakers are already training.
The press secretary says people online debate whether you're "that owner who flies economy." You do — whenever the jet breaks.
The airline wants a fifth plane. A seller offers a used one that "hardly flew." That's more alarming than reassuring.
The coders built a chat for the whole holding. The first message is from a baker: "How do I bake bread in here?"
Your aunt wants her son taken on at the club, "even just on the bench." He's forty-five and last played at school.
left: Invite him to a veterans' match

text: The lawyer says buying the cinema got you a collection of old film reels. A museum wants to buy them; film buffs beg you to keep them.
Your assistant found "lunch with someone important" in your calendar. Nobody wrote down who. The table's booked in your name.
Your hotel is hosting a conference for your software firm's competitors. The director asks if anything should be "accidentally overheard."
right: Send a coder to the coffee break

text: The toy factory released a "Build your own holding" set. It's missing a "time off" piece.
You're finally on the jet. The pilot: "Off in twenty minutes. Probably." Five hours later you're still waiting. Enough?
right: Wait and work from the cabin

text: Your daughter wants a school fair selling buns from your bakeries. "You'll give me a discount, right?"
Scrolling your channel's news at night, you learn your club signed a striker. You never approved it.
The head baker sends a photo of the first loaf made from flour off your own farm. "This bread is the whole holding."
Your spouse asks why you're going to the ski resort "for work" again this weekend. You don't even own skis.
Late at night the media director calls: "Our site crashed from traffic. The story: you ate street food by the station."
right: Ask them not to blow it up

text: The club director invites you to watch the youth squad's evening training. He says there's a "future star."
The treasurer needs 140 payment orders signed before midnight. The e-signature's down. Pen only.
Your nephew, the club cashier, hasn't complained in a month and even sped up the queue. He asks for a promotion.
The laundry director invites you to their party. You've never set foot in any of your laundries.
In the evening, a former foundation scholar calls: he landed his dream job and wants to say thanks. The call runs long.
left: Listen as long as he needs

text: You realise every hobby you've had turned into a company. You nearly bought a chess club last week.
Your assistant asks whether to send holiday greetings to the directors on your behalf. "Or will you write them?" There are twelve.
The bookshop director asks you to host the evening book club. The first book is about the harm of overwork. You haven't read it.
The coders invite you to their all-night hackathon: "The owner should write at least one line." You last coded at school.
The ski resort manager asks to let kids from the sports school ski free in the evenings. That's lights and lift time.
In the directors' chat, an argument over whose company is "the main one" enters its third hour. Everyone awaits your word.
7 a.m., from the bakery director: "Why does the club have a sports psychologist and we don't? Bakers worry about dough too."
Your alarm rings on the airline phone, then the club phone, then the bakery phone. Three alarms, one of you.
The pilot cheerfully reports the jet's ready today, but the airport's closed by fog. "On the bright side, fresh coffee."
Your son asks if he can bring friends to your box at the match. Twenty-two friends. The box seats eight.
left: Buy them seats in the stands

text: At 6 a.m. the farm director sends a video: a cow walked into the office and lay down on the reports. "We'll miss the quarterly."
right: Ask for photos of the pages

text: The editor says the morning edition will run without the owner's column since you never sent it. It's 7:50. Deadline's 8:00.
HR wants all company directors to take one leadership training. The club director asks if there'll be balls.
The treasurer suggests cutting the jet's Wi-Fi to save money. "You don't work on it anyway — you wait on it."
right: Keep it, in case we ever fly

text: The software CEO sent a plan: AI to schedule your day. Its first move was to schedule you a rest.
The captain texts: "Can we wear bakery T-shirts to training today? We're fans." The club's sponsor won't love it.
right: Ask them to wear them after

text: Your mum shows up at the office with a pie "for all your directors." Twelve directors. One pie.
The airline director wants morning flights to leave fifteen minutes early "so they arrive on time."
right: Fix the real cause of delays

text: The driver suggests bringing a thermos to the club meeting. "Their coffee is awful, I remember."
right: Drink the awful stuff with everyone

text: The laundry buyer wants to come in the morning and count how many machines are spinning at once. "Better than any report."
The hotel director replaced bottled water with jugs. "Eco-friendly." Guests are already reviewing the missing bottles.
Your niece applied to the software firm. She signed her CV with your surname in large letters.
left: Ask her to sign it normally
right: Pass it to HR as is

text: The board proposes a yearly "holding day" where all companies show off their wins. Budget: a small concert.
right: Keep it modest, in the canteen

text: Your club reached the next cup round. The opponent is sponsored by a rival holding. The press calls it "the battle of the owners."
right: Promise to be in the stands

text: The bakeries won "best bread in the city." The director asks you to collect the award on stage. He clearly wants to himself.
An investor wants a stake in the club — if it moves to another city. "More fans there."
The auditor asks why your media company pays more than anyone else to advertise your own club. "A friends' price, in reverse."
At lunch you look at your to-do list. Eighteen items. Number seven: "have lunch." Skip it?
left: Have lunch, it's on the list

text: The software CEO wants to rename the firm to something trendy with no vowels. The media director says it can't be pronounced on air.
The toy factory wants to make models of your airline's planes. The airline director asks that the models at least arrive in shops on time.
You've been invited to the opening of a rival bakery. With a note: "We'd love your advice."
The coach wants summer training at your ski resort: "Altitude, fresh air, goats."
Your uncle wants your channel to air his accordion contest performance. It's a news channel.
Your outlet published a ranking of "the best business owners." You're number one. It looks suspicious.
The CFO suggests selling the ski resort while there's no snow: "Buyers assume there'll be some." That's a bit dishonest.
The laundry director offers to wash the club's kit for free — in exchange for a logo on the shirts.
The flight attendant asks you not to eat lunch on the jet while it's parked. "It looks weird from the apron."
Fans came to the holding office singing "Owner, buy a goalie." Catchy song. Good rhymes.
Your cousin's café is closing and she asks you to buy it. "You buy everything anyway."
Evening. The club won the cup! The director invites you to the dressing-room party. At 7 a.m. you're negotiating the laundry sale.
Your daughter asks why you own five companies but only made it to the second act of her play.
You get home and realise you didn't answer a single friend all day. Only directors.
right: Reply to everyone with an emoji

text: The pilot texts in the evening: "We're definitely flying tomorrow. I fixed everything myself." Not sure that's good news.
Late evening: the editor asks you to approve a story on how your bakeries throw away unsold bread. It's accurate.
Watching your channel at night, your spouse asks why it's the third story about your club. "Isn't that a bit much?"
left: Ask the editor to balance it

text: The airline director says a passenger left one of your factory's toys on a plane, and a child is crying. The plane's in the hangar.
The treasurer sends one line in the evening: "Did we sell the ski resort?" You didn't. Or did you?
The coders pushed a bakery app update tonight. Every bun now costs zero. Customers are delighted.
The foundation calls: your anonymous donation made the news — on your own channel. The editor "didn't know."
left: Ask them to remove your name

text: Your brother invites you fishing this weekend. Saturday you're viewing a new hotel; Sunday it's the club board.
Your assistant asks if you'd like a gift for yourself after a good year. "Just not a company, please."
The toy factory reports your "Holding Owner" doll sells worse than the "Bakery Director" doll. The bakery director already knows.
right: Make a joke in the group chat

text: Sunday evening. You start thinking about Monday at all five companies at once. Your tea's going cold.
The ski resort manager sends an evening photo: snow at last, and the first skiers are your own bakers on a team outing.
The bookshop director asks if they can stock your upcoming book. You're not writing a book. Yet.
Late at night, the hotel manager writes: "I get it now! I decide. I've decided to replace all the curtains." Pricey curtains.
right: Ask him to clear big spends

text: You did end up buying a small print shop. Its director asks what to print first: business cards for all your directors, or club posters.
The club director needs ticket prices signed off. Raise them and the budget breathes. Keep them and the fans are happy, the club isn't.
The bakery and software directors both sent you the same proposal: "Merge our marketing teams." Each wants to lead it.
In the mirror you notice your jacket has a club badge, a software-firm lanyard, an airline pin and a croissant stain.
The airline director wants you at the new route's launch. You'll have to fly a competitor, since your own plane won't be ready.
The pilot apologises: the jet's late again, "but for a good reason this time." It's the dispatcher's birthday.
The editor asks if the site can run ads for your own bakeries. "Otherwise the sales team cries."
The family office asks which companies should one day pass to your kids. The kids only want the cinema.
The farm director writes: "Can we name the new calf after you? He's very stubborn."
The foundation asks you to join the 6 a.m. bread handout. The bread is from your bakeries. You are very sleepy.
A new coder found a bug in the club's app: it's selling tickets for 1998 matches. He wrote to you directly.
The bakery director arrives at 8 a.m. in a tracksuit the club gave him. "I want to be closer to football."
The coach calls early: "I have a season plan but I need your view." You look at a ball and see a ball.
Your sister writes that her column at your outlet outreads the news. She wants a promotion to "chief columnist."
The driver suggests taking the metro to work for once. "They say it beats the traffic."
The laundry director reports machines in one shop are spinning in rhythm. Customers are filming it. Charming or breakdown?
The treasurer wants every company's payday on one date. "Convenient." Footballers prefer another day.
Your media outlet wants an interview with your own football club. The club refuses: "You criticise us."
The lawyer says the cinema deal needs twenty signatures. Your pen ran dry. It's an airline-branded pen.
The club director wants to change coaches mid-season. The coach already knows and is standing behind the door.
A rival holding released their own "Owner" doll — with a jet that arrives on time. Their sales are higher.
You've been invited onto a TV show, "A day with the owner." A camera will follow you from morning to night.
The head baker asks for leave at the peak of holiday cake season. "Haven't had a break in twenty years."
right: Ask him to wait a month

text: The factory wants to make balls for your club. The players tested one: it bounces, but sideways.
You catch yourself telling the airline director "in the bakeries we solved it like this." He looks puzzled.
The airline pilots learned the jet pilot earns more. They're writing a joint letter.
A buyer offers a swap: your print shop for his bike rental. "I need printing, you need a ride."
Your assistant asks which director sits next to you at the investor dinner. Every director has already asked personally.
The software firm wants a hackathon for the whole holding. The bakers ask if they can hack the oven.
The CFO warns: the laundries made almost all the holding's profit this year. "Maybe make them the flagship?"
The foundation wants to set up an award in your name. You dislike named awards, but they think it'll bring more donations.
Your dad's touring the software firm and asking coders when they'll "finally make a proper phone."
The hotel director wants a "History of the Holding" exhibition in the lobby. Star exhibit: your first calculator.
Your aunt sends a photo from your plane: "Flew with you — long wait, but great food!" Best review of the year.
9 p.m.: the club director asks if you'll attend tomorrow's press conference on the new coach. You haven't decided you need one.
Your spouse is cooking and asks you, just once, not to talk about the laundries at dinner. You were about to.
You get home and automatically say "good morning." It's 10:40 p.m.
The editor says the evening news is pushed back an hour for your club's live match. The news will wait.
Your daughter wants a bedtime story on video from the jet. It's been on the runway two hours already.
The airline director writes at night: "The flight landed on time! Can I be late to tomorrow's meeting?"
right: Ask him to be on time

text: The treasurer sends evening charts with every company in a different colour. The holding looks like a rainbow, but one stripe is falling.
Your nephew sends a photo: he's been made senior cashier. Can he wear a club-logo tie now?
The bakery director invites you to the night shift: "See where it all begins." That's at 11 p.m.
Your brother asks to borrow the jet for his holiday. It's just been fixed.
After a loss, fans wait for you at the stadium exit. Twenty of them, in scarves, looking stern.
The software CEO writes: "We finished the release. Can we all skip tomorrow?" All forty of them.
Your assistant suggests a night-time auto-reply: "The owner is resting." The club director calls that weakness.
You remember you started with one tiny bakery. Life was simpler. Money was nonexistent.
The cinema director proposes a late-night screening for staff of all your companies. The vote picked a movie "about planes."
Evening call from the farm: the calf named after you escaped and is wandering the next village. Reporters are already there.
right: Have the press office joke about it

text: The morning flight's cancelled by a storm. Passengers are angry. The airline director wants to hand out bakery buns on the holding's tab.
The lawyer suggests gathering the family this morning to discuss who runs the holding "someday." The kids are at school, your brother's on holiday.
No meetings until lunch today. Suspicious. Maybe your assistant forgot to add something.
The bakery director declared war on the laundry director at dawn: "They take too long washing our café tablecloths."
The captain asks you to come to the kids' open training and show your kick. Everyone remembers that penalty.
Your assistant asks how "morning meditation, 5 minutes" got into your calendar. You didn't add it.
The editor asks you not to call the newsroom in the mornings. "Not even to praise. Journalists get nervous."
The factory director asks if staff's kids can join the morning floor walk. "They want to see what their parents do."
The cinema buyer calls at 7:30: "I've changed my mind. But maybe you'd buy my swimming pool?"
First time in a year, the pilot announces: "We're twenty minutes early." Nobody's there to meet you yet. Wait on board?
HR proposes a "no-directors day": each company runs itself for a day. The directors are offended.
Your cousin writes: "I signed up for cabin crew training! Can I work on your jet?"
The farm grew a pumpkin the size of a car. The director wants it delivered to the holding office "for inspiration."
6 a.m., from the coach: "Found a goalkeeper. He works at your laundry. Catches socks mid-air."
Mum sent a seven-minute voice note about spotting your plane in the sky. "It flew so straight!"
The coders want the workday to start at eleven. "The brain doesn't compile before eleven."
The CFO suggests selling the jet and buying a share in someone else's. "Then someone else's jet will be late, not yours."
The club and media directors fell out over the word "mediocre" in a match report. Both want to meet you at once.
The banker proposes buying a florist chain: "Synergy with the bakeries — bread and flowers!" You don't see it.
Your hotel got a bad review: "Too many football club logos." The hotel director blames the club director.
At lunch you realise you know all your directors by name but not their deputies. And deputies become directors.
right: Ask for a list with photos

text: The head baker returns from leave with a new loaf: "The Rested One." It genuinely looks perkier.
The lawyer says the laundry buyer wants the director included in the deal. The director doesn't know yet.
Your uncle opened a bakery opposite yours. "Competition is healthy." His sign is a copy of yours, with a typo.
Your channel wants a documentary about your holding. You're not sure you want your mornings on screen.
The board suggests every director hang your portrait in their office. "It's customary." You feel awkward.
The laundry director heard about a possible sale and asks directly: "Are we being sold?"
The foundation wants a bus for a children's choir. The club director offers the old team bus, "with history."
Your assistant found a free hour and suggests a nap. The airline director just texted "got a minute?"
The software firm wants to sell its app platform to competitors. Good money, but your bakery app runs on it.
The cinema wants free matinees for pensioners. The director asks to approve "a small loss."
Three days into his summer internship at the software firm, your son proposes a new logo. Everyone silently looks at you.
The press secretary asks how to answer rumours you're buying a circus. You're not. You only looked.
Evening: the airline director says the pilots are striking tomorrow. The reason: the new uniforms are too itchy.
First movie in a month. Halfway through you realise it was shot in your hotel.
Your spouse finds three purchase contracts in your bag. "You promised not to buy anything this month."
The captain texts: the team wants to bring the farm cat to an away game. "He's lucky."
The toy factory got an evening complaint: its balls bounce sideways on your club's pitch. The club director is furious.
The treasurer asks: "Can the hackathon pizza go on the bakeries' budget? It's dough, after all."
Your sister calls late: another outlet reprinted her column and now she's "in demand." She wants to leave for them.
Your assistant asks whether to book a family dinner this weekend. You've cancelled three times already.
At 11 p.m. the editor sends ratings: the week's top story is your pilot feeding pigeons by the jet.
The foundation's evening report: you helped two hundred families this year. At the bottom: "Did you rest even once?"
The club director wants you at dinner with a new sponsor. It's a fast-food chain, and your bakers will be hurt.
Your daughter wants to teach you a video game where you run a holding. You're better at it in the game.
The farm director's evening list: a tractor, a barn roof, and "a little attention from the owner." The last one's free.
right: Pay for the tractor and roof

text: At 11 p.m. you catch yourself reading bakery reviews. One says: "Tasty, but the cashier looks sad."
left: Find out how the cashier is

text: The resort manager suggests holding the company New Year party on the slopes. "Everyone rides up on the lift." The lift is old.
left: Hold it by the fireplace below

text: The bookshop director wants a video of your reading recommendation. This year you've only read reports.
right: Admit it and ask for tips

text: Your brother asks in the evening if you'd just sit in the kitchen without a phone. "Like we used to."
The jet mechanic calls at 6:40: "Found the cause of the delays. A nest in the engine. The birds moved out and left a note." He's joking, but departure's late again.
The architect presents the new HQ: one floor per company, and your office on the roof. "Overlooking everything."
left: Put me on a shared floor

text: The bakeries opened, but one has no bread: the flour truck is stuck. The director asks if he can sell yesterday's loaves "discounted and honestly."
The barista at your hotel café recognises you and offers coffee "the way the owner likes it." You have no idea how you like it.
The club director sends morning news: your striker appeared in an ad for a rival holding. In boots in your club colours.
You planned to work from home, but there's renovation noise next door. Your neighbour runs your print shop.
A courier dropped off forty boxes of uniform samples for all your companies. Pick by lunch.
The airline director proposes announcing the owner's name at each take-off. "So passengers know who to write to."
right: Announce it with an email address

text: The family office reports your kid invested pocket money in a rival's shares. And did rather well.
The editor says the evening anchor is leaving. Your cousin wants the slot — he has "a good radio voice."
The hotel director asks if the rival team can stay free before the match. "It's hospitality." The club director objects.
Your trainer suggests a run around the stadium with the team. The team runs fast. You, not so much.
The cinema wants morning cartoons for staff kids from all companies. The popcorn comes from your bakeries. It's slightly burnt.
Your assistant asks which director you'll praise publicly today. "It's our Friday thing." You want to praise them all.
The foundation got a request from a school: thirty computers. Your software firm happens to be replacing its old ones.
Your niece got into the software firm on her own, without your help. She doesn't want you to tell anyone.
The toy factory wants a board game called "The Late Jet." Your jet pilot is offended and won't give his photo.
An investor offers to fund your club if his son plays in the first team. The son is sixteen and genuinely decent.
The bakery director insists his report goes first at the holding meeting. "Last time football went first."
The lawyer says you accidentally bought the rights to an old song fans sing at the stadium. Now they need your permission.
The media director wants more money for the website. The bookshop director wants free ads on it. Both look at you.
Mid-lunch, "Urgent!" lands in three chats at once. Bakery, club and foundation. Spoon frozen mid-air.
The dispatcher asks if a flight can wait ten minutes: your own club director is running late. A hundred passengers are on board.
The laundry director learned the sale is off and sent a cake reading "Thank you." From a rival bakery.
The board wants you to stop personally answering fan letters. "Not owner-level work." You answer five a week.
right: Hand it to the press office

text: You're offered a small pet shop. The seller says: "Your holding lacks something alive." You own a farm.
The software firm built an app to rate your boss. The bakery director scores 4.9. You score 3.7.
Your aunt toured the print shop and asked for a hundred postcards with your face on them "for the relatives."
The club director wants to hold a press conference at your hotel. The hotel director charged full price for the room: "Business is business." Both message you.
The jet's flight attendant asks if the idle jet can be used to train airline trainees. "It's just sitting there anyway."
A chart of your holding hangs in the meeting room. You're seeing it whole for the first time. An arrow points to a company called "Daisy."
Your assistant asks if he can sometimes work from home too, like the coders. Without him your day falls apart.
Evening: a big club wants your young star for good money. He's your best player.
Your spouse suggests a holiday at your hotel. "We know the place." You fear you'll spend it inspecting towels.
In the evening, the head baker admits he'd love to try football. "Just once, on a real pitch."
Before bed you check the share price, the weather for the airline and the match score. You forget to check on sleep.
Your daughter asks you to teach her percentages. You explain using holding stakes. She's bored.
Late message from the airline director: "A passenger left a cat on the plane. The cat's fine but refuses to leave."
The farm director's evening voice note: "The flour's ready. Can we deliver it to the bakeries ourselves? By tractor?"
The treasurer reports the foundation underspent this year: "There's money left." Directors are already pitching ideas.
Late-night call from the editor: "There's an error in your column yesterday. You mixed up your own company names."
Your cousin finished cabin crew training and works his first flight on your airline. He asks you to come aboard for moral support.
Charity concert night. You're invited on stage to sing with the choir. You can't sing.
Your assistant sends tomorrow's schedule: "Day starts at 5:40. Sorry."
The hotel director calls: at a company party, bakers and coders are arguing over who's first on karaoke.
You count how many times this week you said "I'll be quick." Thirty. You were never quick.
The bike rental director — you got the business in exchange for the print shop — wants free bikes for all holding staff. The pilots are eyeing a tandem.
The bike rental director sends an evening photo: the bakery and club directors riding a tandem together, apparently reconciled.
left: Post it in the group chat

text: In the evening your son asks: "If I don't want to run the holding, will you be upset?" He looks very serious.
In the evening, the jet pilot admits he fears being fired over the delays. Twenty years at the controls.
The morning starts with: "Someone tried to hack the holding's email. It failed because your password is 'bakery123'. Nobody guessed it."
Morning video call with all directors. The farm director has a cow behind him, the pilot clouds, the editor chaos. You're in pyjamas.
Your outlet's site ran a morning story: "Holding owner buys an island." You bought a tiny island in a park pond — for ducks.
Your assistant installed a smart speaker. At 8:00 it reads your schedule aloud, including "time for a little cry" at 3 p.m.
The bakery app sent every customer a morning notification: "Your bread has gone cold." Nobody had ordered anything.
right: Have the coders fix it quietly

text: A new coder proposes putting the whole holding on one accounting system. "Only six months." The seniors laugh.
left: Let him pilot it in one company

text: The press secretary wants you on social media. "An owner without a profile looks suspicious."
You woke up to find you replied to the airline director overnight with one word: "Hooray." You don't remember to what.
The airline wants app-only ticket sales. Elderly passengers keep calling to ask where the app is.
The treasurer wants digital reports only. The farm director sends his as a photo of a notebook page.
The club director wants to sell digital player cards. Fans doubt they need "pictures for money."
Mum has mastered video calls and rings every morning at 8:15 "just to look at you." That's when your stand-up is.
The hotel installed smart curtains. They open at 5 a.m. and won't close. Guests complain about forced sunrises.
Your nephew made a club video with a million views. In it he's dancing at the ticket desk. The club director can't decide whether to scold or praise.
right: Ask for one about the team

text: Your fitness band shows three hours of sleep. Your trainer sees it in the app and cancels the session.
The editor wants a new website. Your software firm offers a "family price." A freelancer promises cheaper and faster.
HR proposes AI screening for hiring across the group. In a test run it rejected your head baker.
A rival holding launched an all-in-one app. It copies your software firm's idea, even the bun on the icon.
You realise you're subscribed to every company's newsletter. Twenty emails a day with your own news.
The factory made a talking pilot toy. It says: "Departure delayed." The airline director demands the line be cut.
The lawyer warns your bakery app collects too much customer data, including favourite fillings. It's excessive.
The media director wants a podcast where your company directors debate each other. Episode one: "Bread vs Football."
right: Don't pit them against each other

text: Your assistant accidentally posted your personal to-do list in the directors' chat. It includes "figure out why I own a farm."
Having seen your list, the farm director sent a forty-slide deck: "Why you need a farm." Slide forty is a cow.
A big tech corporation wants to buy your whole software firm. The coders learned from the news and are messaging you directly.
The bakeries introduced pay-by-face. The first person it failed to recognise was the bakery director. He wasn't smiling.
The CFO wants identical laptops for all directors. The software CEO calls them "laptops for grannies."
The team captain started a behind-the-scenes blog. Mostly lovely, but there's a clip of you dozing off in a meeting.
The software firm offers a chatbot to answer your email. In testing, it was too polite: it agreed to everything.
The foundation suggests an online drive where you personally thank every donor. Two hundred donations in an hour.
The hotel wants app-based room keys. In testing, the hotel director got locked out — on a balcony.
right: Rescue him, then improve the app

text: You look at the holding dashboard. Everything's green except "owner's mood." Someone in tech added it.
Your outlet is launching a paywall. Your mum is already asking whether she gets it free.
Evening: the bakery app crashed because everyone ordered match-day pies at once. "A good problem to have."
right: Ask for a fix by morning

text: Scrolling in the evening, you see a stranger praising your airline. You want to like it. That would be weird.
Your spouse finds six of your companies' apps on your phone and asks if one could go.
The club director sends a replay of a disputed goal. You watch it ten times and still can't tell if it was offside.
The pilot sends you a jet-tracking app. On the map the jet sits in a hangar, labelled "sleeping."
Your daughter recorded a video parodying you in a meeting. Her friends love it. You recognise yourself a bit too well.
right: Ask her not to post it

text: 10 p.m.: "We've got a leak about your rival. Run it?" The leak looks dubious.
Your assistant set do-not-disturb on your phone from 10 p.m. to 7 a.m. The airline director found out and is hurt.
The bakery director sends a bread recipe invented by AI. Raisins, cheese and mint.
Drifting off, you remember you didn't charge your laptop, phone or watch. Three chargers, one socket.
right: Get up and rig an extension

text: The captain's club blog took off and advertisers are calling. "Can I advertise your bakeries?"
right: Ask him to keep them separate

text: The foundation sends a video from the kids' coding school: they made a game where you chase a late jet.
The editor says comments under the club article have turned toxic. Disable them or moderate all night.
Your brother texts: "I bought shares in your software firm. If they drop, it's on you."
Late evening, the airline director demos new online check-in. Passengers pick a seat and a "flight mood."
The cinema launched evening online screenings. The first viewer is your dad, typing in the chat: "Where's the sound?"
A board member forwards an article: owners who never rest make worse decisions. No comment attached.
At 9 p.m. the banker sends a "final offer" for the laundries. The third final offer this week.
Evening maths: selling the jet would pay the bakers' night bonuses for a year. The thought won't go away.
The ski resort buyer calls at night asking for a discount because "the goats look unfriendly."
The treasurer finds one company has paid five years for a subscription nobody uses.
Your sister asks for a loan for her handmade-candle business. The business plan is one page, but pretty.
The club director wants to sell stadium naming rights to a soda maker. Fans will end up singing about soda.
Your spouse suggests making a family budget "like normal people." You own a holding and don't know what milk costs.
Evening: an advertiser is leaving because the outlet criticised its product. That's a third of revenue.
Evening call: a big retailer wants your toys — below cost. "But think of the volume!"
The bank emails at night: "You're our best client!" and offers a credit card with cashback on jets.
right: Sign up, it's a good deal

text: The bakery director confesses one shop has lost money for three years — it's in his parents' building.
The auditor finds the club's "fan gifts" line is seventeen thousand scarves. They're in a warehouse.
Your cousin's café survived and paid its debt to your bakeries. She invites you to a celebration dinner.
The hotel director wants to double room rates on match days. The club director objects: "Fans will be upset."
In your jacket you find an airport coffee receipt. It cost as much as lunch. You were waiting for the jet.
Your daughter set up a lemonade stand. Tonight's report: more profit than the cinema made today.
The airline director proposes selling one plane and leasing out another. "Smaller, but on time."
The CFO arrives at 8:00 with good news: a profitable year. And bad: the directors already spent the profit.
The club director asks the bakeries for an advance. "We'll pay you back when we win the cup." The cup is six months away.
You realise your owner's salary is lower than the airline director's. You decided that yourself three years ago.
An investor wants a stake in the bakeries and promises "not to touch the recipes." The recipe clause is in small print.
Your assistant asks about the airline's client-gift budget. The director suggests toy planes from your factory.
The treasurer proposes no more printed annual reports. The print shop director is in shock.
The farm beat its harvest target. The director wants to sell the surplus to your bakeries' rivals. "Money doesn't smell of bread."
The family office suggests putting some money into bonds "for later life." You don't feel old. Yet.
HR says the coders are the holding's top earners. The bakers worked out how much that is in buns.
The pilot brings the fuel bill and admits the jet flew to an air show "for reputation." Without you.
The media director wants a new studio. The old one is a former storeroom that smells of pies.
Dad's morning advice: "Don't put all your eggs in one basket." You have eight baskets and still worry.
The hotel director wants a loan for a pool. The payback calculation says it'll pay off by his retirement.
Accounts asks how to book three goats. They came with the ski resort; the resort was sold, the goats weren't.
The board wants a dividend. Company directors want the money reinvested. All eyes on you.
You're offered a lighthouse. A real one, on the coast. The seller: "It's not a business, it's a story." It really isn't a business.
The lawyer says the laundry sale collapses if the director leaves. She's already interviewing elsewhere.
The bakery director pitches franchising. Your recipes would be baked in other cities by others.
You realise you can't buy a bun from a vending machine: only large notes and holding cards.
The factory needs a new production line. The cheap one is fast but loud. The expensive one is quiet, and workers want it.
The software firm found a client who'll pay a year upfront. It's your bakeries' biggest rival.
Your aunt wants to buy one share "as a keepsake." The lawyer will need forty pages.
The pilots offer to give up bonuses to save the fifth plane. The director is moved. So are you.
A journalist asks how much you earn. The press secretary is frantically signalling "don't answer."
A rival proposes splitting the city: your bakeries north, his south. Convenient — and also collusion.
The cinema proposes buying rights to screen the cup final. Expensive — but your club might make it.
The foundation got an anonymous donation: a hundred thousand buns. All from your bakeries. Someone's joking.
The laundry director offers to buy the laundries from you over ten years. "I love them more."
Your assistant listed your subscriptions: seven papers, five streaming services, three gyms. You've never been to any gym.
The farm can get an organic grant. There's a thirty-page form. The farm director writes in longhand.
The bike rental director proposes replacing directors' company cars with bikes. "Huge savings." The club director lives out of town.
The head baker shows that butter prices ate all the croissant profit. "Either charge more or use less butter."
The bookshop director wants to open another shop. Book sales are falling, but people come to sit and read.
left: Open it with a bakery café

text: The lawyer brings a first draft of the estate plan. Item one: "Who gets the jet." Nobody in the family wants it.
Over breakfast your son announces he wants to be a footballer, not a club owner. "Owning is boring."
Your daughter wants a summer job at the bakery. The director's already preparing a "junior director" title.
Mum calls in the morning: "You work too much. Come for Sunday lunch. That's not a request."
The family office proposes a quarterly "family council" with a holding report. Your nephew already wants the floor.
For the first time you wonder: what would happen to the holding if you took a year off? Scary and thrilling at once.
Your nephew, now senior cashier, wants a reference letter for business school. He plans to come back "as a director."
right: Ask the club director to write it

text: Your brother wants to be your deputy at the holding. "I'm always around." He is — mostly on holiday.
HR asks to introduce a rule: the owner's relatives can only be hired through open competition.
Your aunt sends a morning list of relatives "who could use help with a job." Two pages.
Dad tells you he worked forty years at one plant. "And you just buy and sell. Where's your plant?"
left: Take him to the toy factory

text: Your spouse opens the fridge: nothing but samples from your companies — farm yogurt, bakery buns and, somehow, a toy plane.
Your cousin, now cabin crew, calls from a flight: "We're delayed. Is this normal in your company?"
The foundation director proposes letting staff's kids observe at foundation board meetings. "Generosity starts young."
Your assistant asks whether to add all relatives' birthdays to the shared calendar. There are forty-three.
The bakery director admits he'd like to buy the bakeries one day. "For my kids."
The board wants a successor named, even in a sealed envelope. "Just in case." Your mind is blank.
Your sister heard your brother was offered a holding role and she wasn't. She calls to find out why.
Your son joined the club academy. The academy coach asks whether to treat him "like everyone else."
Lunch with the kids: they're arguing over who gets the football club. Nobody asked if you're giving it away.
The lawyer warns: if you're ever away or unwell, no one can sign for you. Not even the treasurer.
Your outlet wants a feature on "Heirs to the holding." Your kids don't want to take part.
right: Ask them to leave the kids out

text: Your cousin wants her husband hired as a driver. Your driver has been with you fifteen years and is anxious.
right: Hire him as a second driver

text: The airline director proposes promoting your cousin to senior cabin crew. "He tries harder than anyone."
The software buyer has a condition: your niece must stay on. She's their best coder. She doesn't know.
The family office proposes a "family constitution" — rules on who joins the business and how. Your brother calls it bureaucracy.
The farm director invites your kids to help on the farm in summer. "Let them see where bread comes from."
Your assistant asks who should stand in for you at a shop opening while you sit on a jet that hasn't taken off.
Signing your hundredth letter today, you realise none were addressed to your family.
The coach says your son is genuinely talented. But if he plays here, everyone will assume it's because of you.
The CFO hints that he should be considered as successor. "I have every number in my head."
Your uncle turns up with a cake asking why he isn't in the "family constitution."
HR proposes mentoring: each director grows a successor. The club director asks whether his cat counts.
In the evening your daughter asks why you have so many companies but no time for her football practice.
The lawyer's evening question: "If the kids don't want the holding — sell or hand it to managers?" Answer needed by Friday.
Your son scored his first academy goal. He calls to ask if you saw it. You were in a board meeting.
Your spouse asks if you want the kids to follow your path. You look at five phones on the table.
Your brother's upset tonight: "You hired everyone but me." Not true, but it feels that way to him.
Mum says neighbours ask if you're really "a tycoon." She tells them: "No, just works a lot."
right: Ask her to keep it simple

text: Your niece texts: "They want to keep me after the sale. Did you sell me too?" Joking — but only partly.
Evening, old photos: you, a tiny bakery and a queue of three. Back then it felt like a lot.
The bakery director admits his son wants to work in tech, not bread. "Like yours, eh?"
Your cabin-crew cousin sends a photo: the flight was on time and passengers clapped. "I kept them entertained."
right: Forward it to the airline director

text: Your sister offers: "Let me chair the family council. I'm good at bossing people."
Your assistant asks if you'd like to enrol in "Handing over a business without losing your mind." Evening classes.
Dad calls in the evening: "You've done well. I never said it, but you have." And hangs up.
The foundation director suggests making the foundation a family affair: the kids choose projects. They're nine and thirteen.
The club director hints he'd love to run the whole holding one day. "Football teaches strategy."
You start a letter to yourself ten years from now. First line: "Hope the jet has landed by now." That's as far as you get.
Your aunt sends a family tree where your name has a plane, a ball and a bun drawn next to it.
8 p.m. The jet took off on time but landed at the wrong airport: "It was less busy." Your city is three hours by bus.
The flight attendant offers a blanket and slippers "in case we spend the night on the runway again."
Third city today. You can't tell which time zone your stomach is in. You want breakfast and dinner at once.
Checking in late at someone else's hotel, the receptionist asks: "Aren't you the hotel owner? Can I give you my CV?"
Your airline's evening flight is delayed. You're aboard incognito. The passenger next to you is loudly cursing the owner.
Your assistant asks whether to cancel dinner with partners since the jet hasn't left. They're already seated.
The cab driver recognises you from the news and spends the ride explaining how he'd run your football club.
The jet mechanic calls at 10 p.m.: "Good news: it's fixed. Bad news: it beeps when turning left."
You call home from the airport for the third evening running. Your spouse asks if you should just buy a flat at the airport.
The team is flying back from an away game overnight. Can they use your jet? "It's just sitting there anyway."
The pilot proposes a new ritual: tea with the whole crew before every departure "for calm." That's another half hour.
At the airport you're in a normal queue for the first time in a year. Strangely calming. You could skip to the owners' lounge.
The bakery director learns you're in another city: "Could you pop into a local bakery and check their croissants?"
Your daughter asks for a souvenir "that isn't from our holding." Harder than it sounds.
left: Bring a pebble from the beach
right: Grab a magnet at the airport

text: The treasurer's evening report: twenty-two days travelling this month. Eight at home, nights included.
The airline director wants to call the evening flight "The Owner's Flight" and seat you free. Passengers will expect you on board.
Airport security asks you to open your case. Inside: three phones, a football, a "Holding Owner" doll and a loaf.
6:00. The pilot: "Wheels up in ten minutes!" You're still at home. Yesterday he said midday.
The airline director reports a thank-you note: "The plane was late, but I had time for breakfast at the bakery."
Your assistant asks which time zone to schedule meetings in: yours, the farm director's, or the pilot's, who's who-knows-where.
Morning in a hotel. You forgot your charger, your suit and, apparently, why you flew here.
Your driver meets you at arrivals with a sign reading not your name but "Owner of Everything." People stare.
The attendant asks what to serve for in-flight breakfast: bakery pancakes or farm yogurt. Both directors are on board.
A buyer suggests meeting at the airport between flights. "Forty minutes is plenty." It's forty minutes to boarding.
The editor wants a morning video message from the airport. The departures board behind you shows your flight as "delayed."
The director of your hotel in another city heard you're coming and lined up the staff at dawn. They're exhausted.
Your trainer sent exercises "for people who live on planes." Step one: "Stand up." You've been waiting three hours to board.
Your cabin-crew cousin asks if he can fly home on your jet on his day off. It's flying empty anyway.
The dispatcher asks you not to call him personally every time a flight's delayed. "I already know."
The club director calls at 6 a.m. your time, forgetting you flew east. "Oh, it's night there? I'll be quick." He's never quick.
The airline director suggests a permanent business-class seat "so the owner flies their own airline."
At the airport you find one of your bakeries. Long queue. One cashier. You could hop behind the counter for ten minutes.
A deal partner in another city suggests continuing the talks fishing, "the way we do it here." Your flight's at six.
The treasurer suggests selling the jet's idle hours to other companies. The pilot's offended: "I'm not a cab driver."
The toy factory wants a collection called "Planes that are always on time." The airline director took it as a dig.
Your assistant bought you a neck pillow with the club logo. The airline director asks why not the airline's.
The pilot proposes giving the jet ride to the winners of the foundation's school contest. That's a day of your time.
The director of your hotel in another city offers you the best suite. Newlyweds booked it ahead of you.
The head baker wants to join your trip to see how others bake. Nobody can cover for him.
The club flies your airline to an away game. The flight's delayed and they'll miss the warm-up.
You're eating lunch on the parked jet because it's the quietest spot in the holding. The pilot knocks.
A rival offers to swap jets for a month "to compare." His jet arrives on time.
A journalist asks why an owner who's always late talks about punctuality in interviews.
Your outlet wants a reporter on your next trip — "to show the owner's life." You've nothing to hide, but still.
The foundation asks you to visit a school it supports while you're travelling. It's your only free hour.
The jet's attendant asks to move to the airline: "At least there I actually fly."
left: Let them go, with a reference

text: The farm director calls at 5 a.m.: "You're flying over us, right? Wave! The whole farm is outside." You're flying the other way.
Mum sends a packing list. Item one: "Hat." You're flying south.
The head baker hands you a bag of croissants "for the negotiations." Enough for a whole board.
left: Hand them out at the talks

text: At customs you're asked why you're carrying twenty "Holding Owner" dolls. You're not sure yourself.
You notice you've started calling staff "my people." Sounds like a villain in a film.
An anchor on your channel calls you "a humble owner" on air. You're watching it in your own cinema, in a private screening room.
After closing, the bakery's guard won't let you in: "Even if you're the owner, rules are rules."
Your spouse notices you now order "the usual" at restaurants, and waiters exchange looks. It's your first visit.
The press secretary brings your website bio. It says "visionary." You bought the laundries by accident.
After a win, fans chant your name. The club director whispers: "Wave." The coach is standing in the shadows.
Reading an old interview, you find yourself quoted: "I'll never buy a football club."
right: Post a reply to your old self

text: The foundation director suggests last year's scholar speak at the awards evening instead of you.
Your son says a kid at school told him: "Your parent's rich, so they must be bad." He's upset.
The editor asks whether to report that you gave up your owner's bonus for the bakers. "It's a good story."
The hotel director accidentally put you in the smallest room. He's horrified and offers to move you.
Your daughter asks if you're "an important person." It's for a school assignment.
The treasurer proposes a bronze bust of you for the holding's anniversary. Budget already set aside.
At the banquet the captain toasts "an owner who knows every player's name." You can't remember the goalkeeper's.
Washing dishes tonight, you realise you haven't done it in six months. It's oddly pleasant.
Your brother says: "You've become a different person." You're not sure it's a compliment.
The bakery director admits everyone at the bakeries calls you by first name, not "the owner." He thinks it's disrespectful.
left: Say that's how it should be

text: A journalist asks where you buy clothes. You honestly don't know. The jumper might be your aunt's handiwork.
The club director wants a reserved "Owner" parking space. The groundskeeper usually parks there.
You're in the canteen queue. Staff keep waving you ahead. You don't want to go ahead.
Your outlet's preparing a regional rich list. You're seventh. The editor asks if you'd like to disappear from it.
The factory director asks if the "Holding Owner" doll can be discontinued. "It doesn't sell, but you'll be offended."
You're invited onto the jury of "Entrepreneur of the Year." The press secretary says it's the easiest way to win next year.
Your cousin wants a photo with you for her café. "Captioned: the holding owner eats here."
Your assistant finds you're booked as "guest of honour" at five events at once. Each expects a speech.
You catch yourself telling a cab driver about your holding. He didn't ask.
The head baker asks you to come at 4 a.m. and help knead. "So you don't forget how."
The board wants you introduced everywhere with full title: "founder and chair of the holding." You prefer your name.
An airline pilot announces mid-flight: "The company owner is on board with us." Passengers turn around. You're in the last row.
The bookshop director wants your memoirs by the till. They don't exist, but "people ask."
The foundation wants a plaque with your name on the library. The librarians would rather have new shelves.
Mid-negotiation the buyer says: "I hear you're tough." You've just been serving him pies.
Your channel wants a cooking show with you. You can only make sandwiches with your own bread.
Your sister's column reveals you sold lemonade to neighbours on credit as a kid. True. The board is not amused.
right: Ask her to clear things first

text: Your driver offers to open the car door for you. You've opened doors yourself for twenty years.
A new hire in the lift asks which department you work in. You don't know what to call yours.
You take the tram to work for the first time in years. The conductor asks for your fare. You don't know how.
Your assistant says a partner sent you a gold pen. Your favourite pen is a cheap kiosk one.
The bakers hung your early-days photo in the bakehouse: apron, flour everywhere. The director wants it down: "Not dignified."
The hotel wants to rename its best room "The Owner's Suite." Families usually stay there for the view.
Your trainer suggests running the city marathon in a holding T-shirt. Runners will be overtaking your logo.
HR wants every new intake to meet you. That's forty new hires a month.
Your aunt told the neighbour you "haven't let it go to your head." The neighbour wants proof — come for tea.
The club director wants a banner with your photo at the stadium. "Fans should know the hero."
The editor asks if your photo should be on the anniversary cover. The alternative: the bakers.
Your son asks why everyone at school thinks you drive a golden car. Your car is ten years old.
The laundry director suggests you work a day undercover at a laundry. "You'll learn a lot."
The office barista wrote the wrong name on your cup. You've been answering to "Gene" all morning.
You realise you haven't said "I don't know" to anyone in ages. Even when you didn't.
A courier brings a box marked "Personal — for the owner." Inside, a drawing from a staff member's kid: you, with wings.
Friday evening. You promised yourself no email till Monday. It opened itself — you merely glanced at it.
left: Close it, go for a walk

text: Your spouse bought theatre tickets. At the interval the club calls: the coach is threatening to quit again.
Your trainer texts: "You've missed five sessions. I'm not angry. I'm worried."
You remember you used to love watercolours. The paints have sat in a cupboard for eight years.
right: Buy new ones for the kids

text: Your assistant scheduled "phone-free Thursday evenings." The directors know and now pile everything onto Wednesdays.
Your brother invites you to kick a ball in the courtyard, "like when we were kids." Your players would laugh.
The hotel director offers you a spa weekend in your own hotel. Free. But he'll "just pop in" now and then.
You go to bed at 9:30 p.m. First time in years. The phone buzzes on the nightstand.
Your daughter wants to do a thousand-piece jigsaw together. It'll take all weekend.
The editor wants a story on your hobby. You have none. He suggests inventing one.
The farm director invites you for a weekend. "No reports. Just cows and quiet."
The club director asks why you missed the match. For the first time in a year, you were just asleep.
Mum sends a recipe for "calming pie." It's a regular apple pie.
Sunday evening. You decide not to plan anything. Five minutes later you're planning how not to plan.
Your cousin invites you to his first gig: he drums in a band made up of cabin crew.
The software CEO admits he's burning out and wants a month off. Release is in three weeks.
right: Ask him to hold on till release

text: The treasurer leaves a note on his way home: "The reports can wait. You can't."
Lunch. You decide to walk round the block without your phone. Ten minutes later you're at your bakery's door.
Your trainer suggests training right in the meeting room: "Ten squats before every decision."
HR proposes a mandatory meeting-free lunch break at all companies. The club director asks: "And training sessions?"
Your assistant offers to shift everything an hour so you can eat lunch. Three directors will grumble.
The head baker sees you look tired and silently puts down tea and a bun. Negotiations are waiting.
You count your days off this year. Four. Including the day the jet broke.
The bakery director wants a quiet room for staff in each shop. One oven would have to go.
A board member suggests a three-month sabbatical. "The holding will manage." You're not sure you will.
The bike rental director offers you a bike for commuting. "Twenty minutes and a clear head."
The club director invites you to the veterans' training. "Run around, clear your head." The veterans run better than you.
