You notice it's the third day running you've had the same vending-machine sandwich at the airline. It's not even from your bakeries.
The foundation director proposes a volunteer day at the dog shelter. You love dogs and have never been.
The media director pitches a column: "The owner takes a break." A new hobby every week. Week one: knitting.
Your assistant asks whether to keep a lunchtime slot for "nothing." The airline director has already booked it.
Your sister invites you to a pottery class. "We'll be shaping clay, not companies."
You notice that instead of taking a lunchtime walk you're watching a video about walking.
The factory director gives you a squeezable stress toy shaped like a jet. For when the jet's late.
6:30. The alarm goes off, but it's Saturday. Calendar: "meeting with cinema director." Who put that on a Saturday?
Your trainer suggests a walk in the park instead of a run. "Sometimes that matters more."
Your spouse proposes breakfast together every morning — twenty minutes at least. Your mornings are booked from 6:45.
Your assistant proposes starting each day with ten minutes of silence, no email, no calls. The bakery director's already at the door.
The head baker offers: "Want to learn to bake? Saturdays, no rush."
In the mirror you spot your first grey strand. Or it's flour from yesterday's bakery tour.
The hotel director invites you to rooftop morning yoga with guests. The guests are rival football fans.
Dad's morning advice: "Learn to say no. Once a day." The club director calls with a request.
The airline director invites you to join the pilots on the flight simulator. "Great stress relief."
This morning nothing's urgent: every meeting cancelled itself. That's frightening.
The driver suggests music instead of news in the car. "You know the news — you're in it."
Your cousin invites you to her new café's opening. They serve your bread. You could just sit a while.
The farm director sends a sunrise video over the fields. Caption: "For you. Watch with notifications off."
right: Forward it to the group chat

text: You realise you've had three coffees before eight — each from a different holding company.
Your son proposes a joint "skip day" — no school, no work. You're signing a deal today.
HR suggests giving every director an extra day off "for putting up with the owner."
At 8:00 the airline director arrives with a chart: "We bring the holding prestige." At 8:05 the laundry director: "And we bring money."
Your assistant says directors now arrive before you to be first in line. It's 6:50 and four are in reception.
The club director emails all directors, cc'ing you: "Reminder: the club is the face of the holding." Three have replied-all.
You realise every director thinks theirs is your favourite company. And each is a little bit right.
The bakery director brings you fresh bread every morning. The software CEO noticed and started bringing coffee.
The board suggests a monthly "company of the month." Directors are already secretly campaigning among other companies' staff.
The hotel director asks you not to tell the club director the hotel earned more this quarter. "He's anxious enough."
right: Say it openly at the meeting

text: The software CEO wants to automate every company's reporting. Directors see it as "surveillance."
The laundry director heard the bakery director got a new company car. She arrives this morning by bike "in protest."
The media director proposes a daily interview with one of your company directors. The running order is already disputed.
The treasurer says directors now bypass you and ask him directly for "just a bit more budget."
The farm director's upset: in the directors' group photo he was put at the edge, next to a potted plant.
Directors are pitching projects to the foundation. Each one is "coincidentally" tied to their own company.
The bookshop director writes: "Why does nobody remember us?" You check the company list and find them at the bottom.
At the morning meeting everyone talks at once. You catch the words "budget," "mine" and "football."
The cinema director sent a three-minute presentation video with music. Instead of a report. Everyone else sent spreadsheets.
The board proposes merging bakeries and laundries "for logistics." Both directors stare at each other in horror.
The club director wants to speak last at the annual meeting, "like the headline act."
The airline and hotel directors argue over who houses the flight crews. Each swears theirs is cheaper.
At the all-hands, directors sit in "parties": food by the window, entertainment by the door, tech in the corner.
The bakery director learned the club director got a birthday voice message from you, while he only got a card. The hurt shows even in his report.
Your assistant notices directors ordering lunch from your bakeries to show loyalty. The software CEO orders sushi.
right: Joke about it in the meeting

text: HR reports two directors are poaching each other's staff. A baker left to cook at the hotel.
The software CEO is hurt he wasn't invited to the bakery tasting. "We eat bread too."
The hotel and club directors both ask for "five minutes." Both meetings are about the same car park.
The CFO complains directors ignore his emails but answer you within a minute.
The media director claims hers is the only company that criticises you — so it's the most valuable.
right: Ask her to critique others too

text: You list directors you haven't thanked lately. The list is longer than the list of companies.
The farm director proposes presenting his report on a pumpkin instead of a screen. "It'll be memorable."
The directors secretly ordered figurines of themselves from the factory. All twelve are now on your desk.
The laundry director proposes a yearly one-day company swap. The club director has already picked the hotel.
A board member notes you visit the club more than anything else. "It's in your calendar, and everyone sees it."
The press secretary has three directors' versions of the same news. All want to be the hero.
Your cabin-crew cousin says there's a rumour at the airline: "The hotel is the owner's pet."
In the evening the club director sends a photo of dinner with your rival. "Just a friendly dinner." There's a contract on the table.
The bakery director admits he envies the club director: "They write about him, not us."
Sudden peace in the directors' chat tonight: everyone's praising each other. You suspect they're up to something.
You realise the directors compete for your attention, and you compete for their respect. Everyone's exhausted.
left: Declare a day off for all

text: The hotel director sends a photo: all your company directors having dinner in his restaurant, without you, laughing.
The software CEO suggests a board game with the directors "for team spirit." The game: Monopoly.
The airline director texts: "I hear you're selling the laundries. You won't sell us, will you?"
The media director says directors have started sending the newsroom "news" about themselves. One is about a new tie.
The laundry director learns the sale is off for good and thanks you. "I'll work twice as hard now."
The treasurer proposes one budget for the holding party. Within an hour, every director has sent their own party plan.
Your daughter asks which of your directors is the nicest. You're silent for a long time.
You realise you said "we'll see" nine times today, to nine different directors.
The bookshop director sends you a book: "How to stop comparing." Inscribed: "For your meetings."
right: Gift it to the club director

text: The farm director writes that other directors call the farm "the holding's vegetable patch." He's deeply hurt.
left: Bring the directors to the farm

text: Your assistant admits directors give him gifts to skip your queue. His cupboard is full of chocolate.
The cinema director is upset: he got two minutes at the annual meeting, the club got twenty.
You've put on mismatched shoes: one from the club collection, one an airline gift. You notice only in the lift.
The head baker reports dough "escaped" its tub overnight and took over half a kitchen. The bakers are taking selfies with it.
The farm director sends a photo: a rooster climbed onto the farm office roof and crows straight into the work video call.
Your assistant says there's a 9:00 meeting with yourself. Someone at the software firm set it "as a test."
The rival football team checked into your hotel and demanded your club's flag come down from the flagpole.
Your driver admits he's lost: the satnav insists on routing you to your own laundry.
The factory accidentally made a batch of plush footballs. They don't bounce at all. The director wants to sell them as "office balls."
A pigeon was found in a plane cabin this morning. It's flown three round trips already. Passengers named it.
The editor reports last night's weather got mixed up with the holding's share price. "Tomorrow: sunny, up three percent."
You arrive to find your office has become a storeroom for plush footballs. Only your chair is free.
The treasurer found a "goat expenses" line in the holding accounts. The goats moved to the farm long ago, but the line lives on.
Mum sends a photo from your bakery: "They wouldn't give me a discount even when I said whose mum I am."
The cinema accidentally screened a holding board meeting to kids instead of a cartoon. They watched to the end.
The captain turned up to training dressed as a baker. "Lost a bet to the bakers." The coach isn't laughing.
A new hire sat at your canteen table and is explaining how he hates Mondays. He doesn't know who you are.
Your cabin-crew cousin sends a photo: his old teacher is on board and insists he sing for her.
A sock that's sat in a laundry's lost-and-found for two years was finally claimed. Its owner is weeping with joy.
Your son asks if he can bring a farm goat to school for "My parent's job" day.
The club's mascot — a person in a fox suit — quit mid-match in a huff. The director asks you to wear the suit.
In a meeting you accidentally called the airline director "bakery director." Now both are staring at you.
A man came into a bakery claiming to be you and demanding a free cake. The cashier calls you.
right: Tell them to give him a bun

text: The hotel lift broke and a delegation of investors is stuck between floors. The director is passing them pies through the gap.
Your assistant mixed up folders: at a deal meeting you've opened "New doughnut flavours."
right: Apologise and find the right one

text: The pilot says the jet can't take off: a cat is sitting on the wing. "He won't move. We're negotiating."
Mid-interview in your channel's studio, the backdrop falls. You're now framed by a storeroom full of pies.
The head baker baked a loaf shaped like your face for the anniversary. It's a good likeness. Nobody dares cut it.
right: Donate it to the holding museum

text: A farm cow wandered into a live report on your channel. Ratings tripled.
left: Give the cow her own segment

text: You signed a document — then realised it was a birthday card for the farm director. With your formal signature.
The factory got an order for ten thousand "Bakery Director" dolls. The real bakery director wants a royalty.
right: Explain that's not how it works

text: A passenger left a knitted jumper on board reading "Best pilot." The pilots are arguing over who it's meant for.
The coders launched a bot in the holding chat that posts "The owner is pleased" every hour. Directors are starting to believe it.
A courier delivers a huge cake with no card. Iced on top: "For everything." Nobody owns up.
In the evening you discover you've spent the day with a "Checked. Bakery No. 3" sticker on your back. Nobody said anything.
right: Ask why no one told you

text: The club director reports the fox mascot is back — but now wants a contract and an agent.
Your spouse finds three keys in your pocket, to three offices you don't remember.
The pilot sends a selfie: the cat from the wing now lives in the hangar, "helping" the mechanics. He wants it on the payroll.
The farm director calls: "Can we name a goat after the CFO? She counts everything too."
Your daughter asks why your phone has a contact saved as "Don't answer (club)." She finds it hilarious.
Evening viewers wandered into the wrong screen and watched half a football film instead of a romance. They want refunds.
Your assistant admits he spent the day with your pass and you with his. You got in nowhere; he got in everywhere.
Your channel accidentally ran a bakery ad during a news item about the bakeries. Viewers write: "Too much bakery."
You're trying to remember your bank password. The hint: "Favourite company." You've tried all eight.
The head baker accidentally sends you a voice note meant for his wife: "Get some milk."
Your nephew found a 1987 coin in the club till and is sure it's a sign.
A washing machine "ate" your club goalkeeper's kit. Kick-off's in three hours. No spare.
right: Goalie plays in a baker's outfit

text: Someone rented a tandem and is riding it around the stadium mid-match. It's your brother.
A guard brings back a lost item: your planner, fished out of the hotel fountain. The pages are stuck together.
The airline's pigeon mascot has vanished. Passengers are collecting signatures for its return.
Your brother calls: he was fined for riding a tandem around the stadium. He wants you to pay "as family."
Overnight the "Owner is pleased" bot broke and now posts "The owner is asleep." Directors finally stopped messaging you.
The flour supplier offers a "gift for the owner" — a beach holiday — if the bakeries sign a three-year deal.
right: Take the deal, not the gift

text: The editor reports a journalist found one of your bakeries broke hygiene rules a year ago. It's since fixed. Publish?
right: Ask them to let it lie

text: The club director suggests buying a player through "a friend of the agent," ten percent cheaper. The friend is a dark horse.
An email not meant for you lands in your inbox: every director's salary. You know most, but not all.
HR reports the hotel director rejected a candidate over age. The candidate's filing a complaint.
The factory director wants to save on toy paint. "Kids won't notice." The difference is safety.
The airline director wants to cancel the unprofitable morning flight without warning "if it's under-booked."
The treasurer suggests paying small suppliers two months late. "They're not going anywhere."
A journalist wants a comment on the bakery director's mistake. You can pin it on him or take it on yourself.
A new coder confesses he accidentally deleted the bakery customer database. There's a backup, but the seniors don't know.
The farm director wants to label everything "farm-fresh," though half the milk is bought in. "Everyone does it."
A bank offers a great loan if you move staff salary accounts there. Nobody would ask the staff.
Your cousin wants the same wholesale price as the biggest chain. Her volume: twenty buns a day.
The press secretary suggests buying some glowing reviews for the hotel. "Just a few, to get started."
The bakery director confesses he borrowed from the till to fix his car — and paid it back. Nobody noticed.
Your son saw a classmate cheating. "If I tell, he'll hate me." He wants your advice.
The lawyer found a loophole in the cinema deal: you could skip the final instalment. The seller is elderly.
The hotel director wants to keep a guest's deposit — he "surely" took a towel. There's no proof.
The board wants to halve the foundation to improve the numbers. "Charity isn't business."
An investor will fund the software firm if you fire its founder. "He's holding it back."
You see a cashier at your bakery quietly giving yesterday's bread to a homeless man. Against the rules.
A big advertiser wants its blunder kept out of the news, in exchange for a year's contract.
right: Take it, run a dry item

text: A rival accidentally emailed you their strategy for next year. You could read it.
The coach asks to start the sponsor's son "so the money stays." The kid isn't ready.
The head baker suggests swapping butter for margarine without changing the price. "No one will taste it."
Your assistant can get you a table at a packed restaurant by calling "on behalf of the holding." The queue is two hours.
The laundry director wants lower pay for newcomers "until they prove themselves." Long-timers object.
The laundry buyer is back, offering more if you keep upcoming layoffs from staff until after the deal.
A big donor will fund the foundation if the supported school takes his name. The school objects.
The airline director proposes reselling the seat held for you on every flight. You've never used it.
You realise you promised the club director a bonus for the cup. They didn't win. He hasn't mentioned it.
The editor asks if they can skip publishing an interview with your rival. "He's just a competitor." It's a good interview.
The farm director wants to claim ten extra hectares on the grant form. "Nobody checks."
That evening you remember snapping at your assistant over the jet. He had nothing to do with it.
The bakery director admits he took credit for the head baker's idea in a meeting. Guilt is eating him.
The treasurer finds the holding underpaid tax by mistake. Nobody would notice.
The club director proposes sending rival fans a match invite with the "wrong" kick-off time. "As a joke."
right: Laugh it off, let it go

text: Your brother asks you to recommend a friend of his to the software firm. You don't know the friend.
right: Pass the CV on, no comment

text: Overnight the coders found a security hole in the bakery app. Patch it quietly, or tell customers honestly?
Your spouse notes you promised no evening work this week. It's 10 p.m. and you're working.
A hotel guest left a huge tip by mistake — an extra zero. Staff ask what to do.
Your niece says the software firm's new owner wants to cut pay. She asks you to step in. You no longer own it.
A defect turns up in a batch already in shops. A recall will cost a month's profit.
Your daughter admits she broke a vase at the office and hid the pieces. It was a gift from the board.
The media director suggests buying a blogger's video of your rival being rude to a waiter. "So no one else airs it."
The pilot confesses: half the jet's delays were him waiting for his favourite show to finish.
The foundation reports a grant recipient turned out to be a staff member's relative. The help was genuinely needed.
The airline director wants to blame a delay on "weather." In fact, someone forgot to refuel the plane.
That evening you notice you talked more about yourself than the foundation at the gala. Awkward.
The captain says a player posted something rude about fans. It's deleted, but there are screenshots.
First morning of December. The bakery director reports three times more holiday cake orders than ovens.
The ski resort's new owner calls: "You didn't say the goats open gates." You did.
Morning after the season ends. The club director sends a three-page summer camp plan and a one-page budget. The budget is bigger.
First morning of your holiday. You wake at 6:00 and check messages. Nobody's written. Suspicious.
left: Lock the phone in the safe

text: Summer morning. The airline director says every beach flight is sold out and there aren't enough pilots.
Your assistant asks which directors get New Year gifts and in what order. The gifts are identical.
The morning before New Year. The factory ran out of boxes and is packing toys in leftover hackathon pizza boxes.
The editor wants your New Year message for the channel. "Two minutes max. No reports."
First snow. The farm director sends a photo: the cows are seeing snow for the first time and are frozen in shock. "We need a warmer barn."
January 1st, morning. The hotel is packed and staff are sleepwalking after the night shift.
Mum insists only your bread be on the New Year table, "so the guests know." Twelve guests.
Spring morning. The laundry director says everyone's bringing in winter coats at once. There's a queue outside.
Before the season finale, the captain asks you to say a few words to the team. You've never done it before a final.
Summer morning. The cinema is empty — everyone's at the seaside. The director suggests outdoor screenings.
Before the first school day, the foundation asks you to personally hand out backpacks. Three hundred.
The bookshop director wants a summer reading tent in the park. No budget, lots of enthusiasm.
First day of the holidays: your son asks if he can spend all summer as "assistant coach" at the club. He's twelve.
Spring morning: the bike rental director reports every bike was gone within an hour. People want more.
The board wants to cancel the New Year party to save money. The directors have already bought costumes.
Winter break. The club director wants to take the team to the ski resort. The coach fears injuries.
You're buying family presents on the last day before the holiday. Half the shops are yours. That doesn't make choosing easier.
Bread sales drop in summer. The bakery director wants to sell ice cream. The head baker is aghast: "We're bread people."
Peak holidays, a flight's six hours late. Passengers are singing carols in the terminal. The director wants ideas.
Your assistant asks whether to book your July holiday. The club director has a camp then, the hotel director an inspection.
The hotel is empty in winter. The director proposes a "holding staff week," nearly free.
After the holidays the factory is idle: no orders. The director asks whether to send everyone on paid leave.
The outlet wants a summer feature: "Where the owner holidays." You holiday on your balcony.
Autumn. A record apple harvest. The farm director floats the idea of juice.
The foundation wants a summer camp for all staff kids. Budget: about the same as a small hotel.
HR proposes "summer Fridays": everyone leaves at three. Bakeries are open till nine.
High summer and you're in a jacket at a meeting. Everyone else is in T-shirts. You're chairing.
Your aunt invites you to a village harvest festival. "All the relatives will be there." Forty people with job questions.
The channel wants a New Year concert starring company directors. The farm director is already rehearsing a song.
New Year's Eve, at home with family. At 11:58 p.m. an email arrives: "Urgent, re: club."
Summer evening fan festival. The club director calls you on stage to sing the anthem.
Your spouse wants a holiday somewhere with none of your companies. Hard — your buns are sold even on trains.
Holiday eve. The bakery director calls: "The oven's broken at our biggest shop. Two hundred cakes unfinished."
New Year's evening. The pilot texts: "The jet's covered in fairy lights. Can't fly, but it's pretty."
right: Ask him to take them down

text: Your daughter writes her New Year wish list. Item one: "For you to travel less."
Last evening of the year. The head baker sends a photo: every baker together, floury, tired and happy.
Summer evening: a wedding at the hotel, the restaurant's full. The director asks you to give your table to the newlyweds.
The evening before your holiday. The treasurer sends thirty documents "to sign before you go."
Last evening of your holiday. You realise you didn't think about work for two whole days. A record.
Autumn evening. The farm director invited all holding directors to a harvest party. Only you and the bakery director came.
Your brother invites you to the family's traditional winter yard match. You missed it last year.
Your cabin-crew cousin is working New Year's Eve. He texts: "A hundred passengers here, all singing."
left: Send a greeting to the crew

text: The cinema wants an autumn food-film festival with the bakeries as partner. The bakery director wants it named after them.
Autumn evening: the airline director reports every flight this week was on time — a first in a year. He's crying with joy on the phone.
On New Year's Eve Mum gives you a knitted scarf in the colours of all your companies. It came out very long.
The evening before winter break. Your assistant asks if he can switch off his phone for a week too. Without him you can't even find your keys.
right: Ask him to check in daily

text: You did buy the lighthouse for the foundation. The keeper calls: "The gulls have unionised. They demand fish."
The director of the ice rink you bought "on impulse" last Wednesday asks who you are and what he should do.
The banker sends a list of forty companies for sale. One is the company you sold a year ago.
Your assistant asks if you really bought a ferry crossing yesterday. There's a signed contract in your inbox.
The ferry director says the ferry only sails when the captain's in the mood. Today he isn't.
You wake up thinking: "What if we need a radio station?" You close your eyes and count to ten.
The director of a small tram museum you're being offered takes you on a morning ride. The tram moves at walking pace.
The lawyer warns the ice rink deal comes with a vast stock of two-year-old frozen pizza.
The CFO shows a table: twelve companies now, five profitable.
Hearing about the rink, the club director proposes a hockey team. "We already know how to lose."
The keeper reports tourists want to stay overnight in the lighthouse. "We could rent it as a room." The hotel director is already jealous.
The circus seller calls at 7:00: an elephant named Boris "really wants to join you."
The farm director calls: the neighbour's selling land. "Shall we? We could grow sunflowers just for beauty."
The ferry director wants to sell bakery buns on morning crossings. Six passengers, two hundred gulls.
The family office gently asks whether to adopt a rule: only buy companies after a night's sleep.
The director of a radio station you didn't buy sends you a schedule with an "Owner's Hour" anyway.
The rink director wants morning ice time given free to the sports school's figure skaters. Paid slots are the most lucrative.
You open a shopping app: in your basket — a boat, a mill and a book club. You don't remember adding them.
The board calls an emergency meeting with one item: "Please stop buying everything."
The ferry director wants to combine with the airline: "Fly and sail on one ticket." Both have few passengers.
You're offered a parking lot by the stadium in exchange for the ice rink. The club director is thrilled; the skaters are in tears.
You notice directors now open meetings with: "Before you buy anything else…"
right: Ask them to drop the joke

text: The tram museum offers you a real full-size tram if you help repair their roof.
right: Take the tram for the office

text: The bakery director heard about the lighthouse and demands a bakery there. "People will follow the smell."
The lawyer reports the ferry is registered as a "cultural vessel." It can only carry tours.
Your assistant blocked business-for-sale websites on your laptop. You found out trying to look "just out of curiosity."
The rink's resurfacing machine broke. The director offers to flood the ice by hand with buckets. All night.
The CFO suggests selling the rink, lighthouse and ferry as one lot, titled "Romance."
Your outlet wants a story on how you buy companies. Working title: "The Owner's Shopping Cart."
At lunch the ferry captain agrees to sail daily — if you ride with him and hear his life story.
A rival offers double what you paid for the rink. "I need a hobby too."
HR complains: every new company means new rules, new contracts, new grievances. "We can't keep up."
The keeper wants to host weddings at the lighthouse. First couple: your cabin-crew cousin.
Evening. You're at the edge of the rink you bought, watching kids learn to skate. Best purchase of the year.
The treasurer emails: "If you buy one more company, I quit. With love."
Evening crossing. The ferry director sends a sunset video. No passengers, but what a sunset.
Your spouse asks if you really bought a ferry. "You're scared of water."
The radio seller calls at 10 p.m.: the presenter already recorded a jingle for "Holding Radio."
The rink director invites you onto the ice with the kids' group. You can't skate.
left: Go out and fall with dignity

text: A board member texts: "Heard about the lighthouse. No offence, but you're a romantic genius and a logistics disaster."
Your daughter asks for a little pony. You look at her and realise where she gets it.
The tram museum sends a photo: the tram's restored and decorated with a ribbon bearing your name.
left: Ask them to remove the ribbon

text: You list which purchases actually make you happy. The rink, the lighthouse and the first bakery.
Your assistant admits he secretly talked the circus seller out of calling you. "Sorry — Boris will be happy elsewhere."
The toy factory wants a "Lighthouse, Ferry & Rink" set with an owner figure holding a shopping basket.
The ferry captain calls in the evening: "I only told you half my life story. Continue tomorrow?"
Evening voice note from the club director: "The hockey section signed up forty kids. We need a second ice machine."
The banker writes: "Last chance to buy a dry-cleaning chain. Your laundries would love the company."
The laundry director writes: "Heard about the dry cleaners. If you buy them, I'll run them. But better not."
right: Buy and hand them to her

text: The lighthouse keeper switches on the beam in your honour. You can see it from your balcony.
right: Ask him not to waste power

text: Annual meeting morning. The CFO whispers the report's fine except one footnote: "The jet is our most expensive employee."
You eye the brick-thick annual report and wonder who'll read it. Not even you.
HR brings the all-company staff survey. Top complaint: "too many emails from the owner."
The bakery director gives you the first loaf from the new oven. "For starting with just one shop twenty years ago."
right: Take it home to the family

text: The lawyer brings the final succession plan. You read it through for the first time and realise you feel calm.
right: Go over it with the family again

text: Your assistant shows this year's stats: 412 meetings. Sixty could have been emails.
The club director reports: the first season ever without a loss. He asks you to come to the stadium "just to stand there."
Your son has changed his mind: no longer a footballer, now a pilot. "So the jet lands on time."
left: Take him to the flight simulator

text: The editor wants your year-end interview. Question one: "What would you do differently?"
The pilot announces he's retiring. "I want my last flight to be on time. For you."
The board proposes you become "honorary chair" and hand day-to-day running to a hired CEO.
The farm director sends a photo of the first sunflower in the new field. "Just for beauty, as promised."
The airline director admits he's been offered a job at a major carrier. "But I've grown attached to your four planes."
left: Let him go with your blessing

text: The treasurer's summary: this year you bought no companies Monday to Friday. Only at weekends.
Mum calls: "I read your annual report. Didn't understand a word, but I'm very proud."
The foundation director's tally: this year it helped more people than the whole holding employs.
In the lift, a new hire recognises you: "I joined because you once answered my email." You don't remember it.
Your driver confesses he's wanted to tell you for twenty years: the car window opens. The button always worked.
Final board meeting of the year. They ask for your main lesson. You think of the jet, the bakeries and the goats.
The club director wants to name the new stand after the head baker. "He's fed the fans for twenty years."
At the annual lunch, every director sits at one table without arguing. You can't remember the last time.
The media director sends the year-end edition. Top holding story: "Cat on the jet's wing."
right: Ask to lead with the foundation

text: Your assistant asks what all the staff should give you for the holding's anniversary. "Just don't say 'a company.'"
The head baker asks you to bake bread on stage at the anniversary. "Like on day one."
A buyer offers for the entire holding. Enough that you'd never need to work again.
The hotel director proposes celebrating the anniversary at the hotel, with all directors staying a week together.
Your cabin-crew cousin won "Flight attendant of the year." He wants you to present the award.
right: Let the airline director do it

text: Your daughter's school talk is "My parent." The draft reads: "My parent works a lot, but always tells funny stories."
left: Ask her to read it aloud

text: The CFO wants to sell the ferry now tourist season's over. The captain hasn't finished his life story.
For the anniversary the factory made an "Entire Holding" figure set — every director, the jet and a goat. Record sales.
The coach who threatened to quit weekly a year ago brings you a pennant: "Thanks for not letting me go."
right: Give it to the club museum

text: You realise you can name every director and deputy. Even the goats.
The bookshop director urges you to write that book after all. Working title: "The Jet Runs Late, Life Doesn't."
Last evening of the year. You switch off every phone but the family one. The silence rings.
left: Keep it that way till morning

text: Your spouse asks: "What did you like most this year?" After a long think you say: "Dinner in the kitchen that Tuesday."
The pilot's final flight lands two minutes early. The crew applauds.
The bakery director writes: "Thanks for the year. We never made the news, and that's wonderful."
Your daughter draws you a card: you in the middle, surrounded by buns, a ball, a plane and a goat. Caption: "My holding."
right: Keep it in the family album

text: The treasurer's year summary, one line: "We're alive, and even in profit. Go rest."
Final match of the year. Fans unfurl a banner: "Thanks, owner. But do buy a goalie."
Your brother admits he's proud of you but still doesn't get why you own a ferry.
The foundation director forwards a child's letter: "Thanks for the backpack. When I grow up, I'll start a foundation too."
Your assistant leaves for holiday with a note: "On your desk: a list of what not to buy, who not to call and when to sleep."
Mum calls: "You sound calmer. Is it the holiday?"
The editor asks if next year they can cover the holding without clearance. "Like any other outlet."
Falling asleep, for once you're not counting companies. You're counting sheep. One looks like it's from your farm.
Your son asks if next year he can spend a week at each holding company. "To understand what you do."
The laundry director sends a photo: a year's worth of odd socks from the lost-and-found — a hundred. She suggests sewing a holding flag from them.
On the year's last evening, the head baker calls: he taught your daughter to bake. "She's got a light touch. Not from you."
For once you don't write tomorrow's to-do list. Tomorrow's a day off. A real one.
